prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms are trapped at the magic wavelength, and for its development into a clock with uncertainty near 1e-18 that opens precision tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B046 to B053. My scientific ranking has not changed: the Higgs observation answers a question that the field had asked for half a century, and in that sense it is the more central result. But a prize needs a defensible allocation as well as a defensible discovery, and round 1 showed that nobody, including me, can name three people for B046 without an arbitrary choice among Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra that rests on roles I cannot verify from the supplied material. B053 does not have that problem. All eight opening proposals gave the same pair, Katori and Ye, and the scientific content of the credit is separable: Katori proposed trapping neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice so that the light shift cancels while many atoms are interrogated at once, and Ye's group turned that into the accuracy and many-body programme that reached about 1e-18. The result has been reproduced in several national laboratories, it is mature, and a citation can be written around the lattice scheme and its precision realisation without reaching into the ion-clock or comb prizes. Although I still regard it as a refinement of measurement capability more than a new window on nature, the reach into redshift tests and searches for varying constants gives it a fundamental-physics content that I can describe in the citation without leaning on the prospective redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one my colleagues and I have all voiced: a lattice clock builds on the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlled single ions, and a sceptic can read it as metrology and engineering rather than discovery. I do not think the overlap is disqualifying, because magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a distinct idea, but I accept it is a real cost and that the citation must be narrow. A second cost is credit: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and other clock groups fall outside two names, and I cannot weigh Katori's proposal against Ye's accuracy programme beyond what the supplied text allows. Finally, choosing B053 means that the committee passes over the Higgs experiments again, and I regret that. I would reopen that choice only if a defensible, role-based allocation for B046 can be stated person by person, which round 1 did not produce.

responses.point: Pearce agrees that the Higgs case is overwhelming but says the three-person limit is the binding constraint, and that if the committee accepts the arbitrariness B046 should be in the final discussion with both experiments' founders, while he keeps IceCube as a first alternative because a clock prize does not recognise a new window on nature.
responses.response: I agree with his diagnosis that allocation, not physics, is what blocks B046, and I now draw the conclusion that he stops short of: I have not been given a way to resolve the choice, so I move to B053. His case for including the founders of both experiments is the best available principle, but it leads to four names (Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee, Della Negra) and so exceeds the three-person limit; the limit is exactly what makes the choice arbitrary. On B009, I still regard source identification at 3 to 5 sigma as an opening window and not a completed discovery, and the Halzen, Spiering, Karle allocation remains uncertain, so I keep it out of my alternatives in favour of B046 and B013.

responses.point: Kroll argues that Katori and Ye map cleanly onto a reproduced discovery, that the credit is separable from the 2005 comb prize and ion-clock work, and says B053 is the safer recognition this year if no defensible B046 trio is found.
responses.response: His argument on separability has persuaded me, and it is now central to my vote. What makes the credit separable is the magic-wavelength lattice, not stability or accuracy alone, so I would keep the citation on that scheme and on the 1e-18 realisation. I part from him slightly on framing: I would not present this as the safer option, because that would make the prize a fallback; the reason is that the discovery claim is real and the allocation is clean. I also accept his own caveat that field proximity (his stay in Hall's laboratory) should make us check that the case does not rest on admiration for precision work, which is why I want the fundamental-physics reach in the citation.

responses.point: Lindroth accepts the Higgs importance but cannot support B046 as preferred while the allocation is this contested, and writes the B053 case around the lattice scheme and neutral-atom statistics, while acknowledging that the weight of Katori's proposal against Ye's accuracy programme cannot be settled from the supplied text.
responses.response: I now agree with her on B046 and have moved accordingly. Her point on the relative weight of Katori and Ye is the one open question I take seriously for B053. I would not try to rank them in the citation: the two-name structure with the lattice scheme first, then precision and many-body realisation, keeps both visible without claiming more about priority than the evidence supports. Her emphasis on neutral-atom statistics is a useful addition, but I would put it second to the 1e-18 uncertainty, since the latter is what makes the fundamental-physics tests possible.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a durable organising principle that the 2016 prize did not cover, and says the lattice clock overlaps with earlier prizes more closely than B013 overlaps with 2016.
responses.response: I accepted his trio in round 1 and I still think it is the most defensible core for B013, but I disagree on how to weigh the overlap. The 2016 prize named topological phases and topological phase transitions in its citation, so a reader will see the quantum spin Hall effect as inside that scope even if the specific prediction was not. The magic-wavelength lattice, by contrast, sits beside the comb and ion prizes and does not repeat either. I also keep the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission in view, because their HgTe proposal enabled Molenkamp's experiment and a three-name set cannot cover it. That is why I place B013 as an alternative and not first.

responses.point: Olsson says that choosing three from four for a result achieved by thousands is arbitrary, that a prize this size needs a configuration the committee can justify person by person, and she discloses a conflict on B052.
responses.response: I agree with the standard she states, justify each name individually, and this is the reason I changed my position: I could not meet it for B046 and I can for Katori and Ye. I also think her disclosure of a user connection to B052 was proper, and it is sensible to weight her first place accordingly when the committee counts support. Her own admission that B052 is not obviously more transformative than the correlated-electron candidates, together with the missing Krivanek, Dellby and Zach strand, is a further reason I keep it outside my configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the optical lattice clock as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the citation can say what is new without overreaching into ion-clock work.
How Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy and many-body work should be balanced in the citation, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and other groups are acceptably left out.

Whether a defensible allocation for B046 exists at all, including whether Della Negra should replace Virdee or Jenni; my account of roles at the 2012 announcement is not verified from the supplied material.
Whether the main fundamental-physics payoff of B053 (a redefined second, tests of varying constants) is still prospective, as Eriksson notes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate. My work in string theory and cosmology is not part of any shortlisted discovery, and I have no research connection to optical clocks. This is unchanged from round 1.
